caseno: Appeal from original decree No. 5 of 1966.
lawyer:
Abu Taher Choudhury ----- For the Appellant
Ahmed Sobhan with Md. Fazlul Karim ----- For the Respondent
parties:
Bismillah Oil Mills ----- Defendant-Appellant
Vs.
Messrs Arag Limited ----- Plaintiff- Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiffs case was that in September, 1958 the defendant firm at Chittagong contracted over phone with the Karachi Office of the plaintiff-company for purchase of 14,00. bags of rape-seed, 700 bags at the rate of Rs. 85/7/9 pies and 700 bags at the rate of Rs. 89/15/9 pies per bag of 2 maunds each. This was followed by two letters of the defendant firm dated 18.9.58 and 4.10.58 respectively whereby the defendant-firm asked the plaintiff-company to ship the said goods with mark 'B.O.M.' and send the bills of lading to them. The purchase was a credit purchase and it was agreed that the plaintiff will send the shipping documents to its Chittagong Office and the defendant will retire the documents after paying the price and all charges from the said office. Accordingly the plaintiff shipped 350 bags of rape-seed per "S. S." Mustaii" under bill of lading No. 65 dated 3.10.58, 150 bags of rape-seed per S.S. Anwar Baksh" under bill of lading No. RC. 190 dated 14.10.58 and 350 bap and 550 bags of rape-seed per S.S. "Firdausa" under bills of lading Nos. 129 and 130 dated 6.10.55 and 16.10.58 respectively from Karachi to be delivered to the defendant at Chittagong. As agreed the plaintiff also paid freight and insurance premium for the said consignments on defendant's account and sent the invoices and the bills of lading to its Chittagong Office for being handed over to the defendant on their payment of price freight, and insurance charges as per invoices. When the shipping documents were received by the plaintiff's Chittagong Office, the defendant was noticed to retire the shipping documents on payment of the invoices values But the defendant failed to do so in spite of several reminders and even refused to accept notices As the goods after reaching the Chittagong port were subjected to demurrage and wharf age and as the defendant was not taking delivery, the plaintiff was compelled to instruct the shipping companies to direct their agents to change the name of the consignee in the respective Bills of lading and substitute the name of the plaintiff-company, Chittagong Office in place of the defendant. Thereafter, plaintiff's Chittagong Office again notified the defendant to take delivery under threat of selling the same at market rate at the cost and risk of the defendant. But the defendant did not retire the shipping documents Ultimately the plaintiff's Chittagong office got the said 1400 bags of rapeseed cleared from the Petty and sold the same at Government controlled rate between 14.11.58 and 31.12.58. The plaintiff had to pay clearing charges for the said consignment at the rate of Rs 1/- per bag amounting to Rs. 1400/- and then the total cost added to the amount spent as per invoices stood at Rs. 1,31,289/14 annas. But the same were resold on defendant's account at Rs. 91,534/10 annas. As a result the plaintiff suffered a loss of Rs. 39,152/5/6 pies as per schedule of the plaint and the plaintiff was entitled to recover this amount from the defendant. 

 4. In this case the plaintiff has examined 5 witnesses and the defendant has examined two, P.W. 1 Md Saleh who is an Assistant Manager of the plaintiff-company at Chittagong office has proved the invoice Exts. 5-5(d) which were sent from their Karachi office and has also stated that the plaintiff-firm has sent lawyer's notices Exts. 1(a) and 1(b) to the defendant-firm which they had refused. He has further proved Exts. 2(a) and 2(b) two letters which were sent to the defendant-firm under envelope Ext. 3 P.W. 2 is Sattar Dawood. He is a broker. He has proved Ext. 2(d) and 2(e). Exts. 2(d) and 2(e) dated 18.9.58 and 4.10.58 are two letters written by H.R. Choudhury and Zakir Hossain on the letter-pad of the defendant-firm and with seals of that firm. He has categorically asserted that at the relevant time Zakir Hossain was doing all the business of the mill. In cross-examination it has come out that he used to reside at the house of the proprietor of the defendant-firm from 1958 to the last of 1959, and he Obtained rent-receipts signed by Choudhury Babu and Zakir Hossain. P W. 3 is Rahamatullah Hail Karim. He was examined on commission. He had deposed that the defendant-firm had contracted to purchase in September, 1958 1400 bags (about 2800 maunds) in two lots of 700 bags each rapeseed. The contract had been made over telephone. He has further deposed that 700 bags were sold at the rate of Rs. 85/7/9 per bag of 2 maunds and 700 bags were old at the rate of Rs. 85/15/9 pies per bag of 2 maunds. The contract was for supply of goods F.O.B. Karachi. He has deposed that he received the letters market Ext. C/I and C/2 by the Commissioner (which were subsequently marked as Exts. 2(d) and 2(e) by the Court) signed by Choudhury Babu and Zakir Hossain. He has also deposed that he had paid the freight on account of the defendant firm, got the goods insured and paid the insurance premium on the defendant's accounts. He has further stated that the shipping documents were sent by him to plaintiff's Chittagong office with instruction to hand over the same to the defendant against payment. The defendant did not retire the documents and, there-fore, the plaintiff's Chittagong office on instruction from the Karachi office got the bills of lading amended by getting their names substituted as consignee in place of the defendant and after taking delivery of the same resold the same. He has also state that the plaintiff has suffered a loss of Rs. 39,752/5/6 pies. In cross-examination he has stated that he was instructed by the defendant to send shipping documents to their office at Chittagong and those instructions were given to the plaintiff by the defendant-firm over telephone. He has denied the suggestion that the Karachi office of the plaintiff consigned the goods to Chittagong office in the name of the defendant in order to dispose of the goods in black market. P.W. 4 Abdur Rahman Ibrahim is the Manager of the plaintiff coy at Chittagong. He says that he received the bills of lading of the suit consignment in 1958 and was instructed to realise the dues from the defendant and give the documents to the defendant. There were 4 bills of lading of three ships covering 1400 bags of rapeseed. He has further deposed that the defendant-firm was informed over telephone and also by letters to take the documents after payment but the defendant did not turn up to retire the ship-ping documents. Thereafter, they informed the Karachi office and on being instructed by the Karachi office they got the Bills of Lading amended by substituting the name of their Chittagong office in place of the defendant, took delivery of the goods and after serving lawyer's notice upon the defendant sold the goods The defendant did not come forward to take delivery of the goods. P.W. 4 has proved the signatures of Hridoy Ranjan Choudhury in Exts. 11 and 12 and has also given positive evidence that Hridoy Ranjan was the employee of the defendant. 

 5. Defendant No. 1 is Abul Hossain the proprietor of the defendant-firm. He was also examined on commission. He denies the contract. He denies that the defendant-firm placed orders over telephone. While admitting that Zakir Hossain is his son he says that the son is separate from him for last 20 years and carries on his business in Dinajpur and Rajshahi. He however, says that the sop is aged about 20/25 years only. In cross-examination he says that a man named Hridoy Ranjan Choudhury was his employee about 9 years back. In reply to a question put by way of interrogatives "Is it a fact or not that Zakir Hossain used to manage the Mills in 1958, if not who was the manager of the Mill in 1958" D.W. 1 Ahul Hossain, the proprietor of the firm answered the first part in the negative but in answer to the 2nd part he named Hridoy Ranjan Choudhury to be the Manager in 1958. In reply to another question he has said that his manager had authority to make correspondences. D.W. 2 Md. Hossain is another son of Abul Hossain. He has deposed to the effect that Zakir Hossain his elder brother was separate from his father for 15/16 years. He says that Zakir Hossain had nothing to do with the mill. He goes one step further and says that no person named Hridoy Ranjan Choudhury ever served under his father's mill. In cross-examination he has said that Zakir Hossain works at Rajshahi/Dinajpur but comes to Chittagong at times. This is all the oral evidence adduced by the parties. Coming to the documentary evidence it appears that Exts. 2(d) and 2(e) are two letters dated 18.9.58 and 4.10.58 written on the letter-pad of the defendant-firm by Hridoy Ranjan, Choudhury and Zakir Hossain respectively on behalf of the firm with rubber stamp seal of the firm. In the letters the alleged contract of purchase is admitted including the quantities purchased with price, 700 bags @ Rs. 85/7/9 per bag F.O.B. and 700 bags alias Rs. 89/15/9 per bag F.O.B. Exts. 2(d) and 2 (e) written on the letter pads of the defendant-firm containing signatures of the authors of letters with the seals of the firm prime facie prove that the defendant-firm made the alleged contract with the plaintiff and the authors of the letters had authority to confirm the contract and request for shipment. D W. 1, the proprietor of the firm has deposed in the case but he has not denied that Exts. 2(d) and 2(e) were on their letter-pad and the seals in the letters were theirs. Ext. 5 series prove that the invoices were prepared in the name of the defendant-firm and in the invoices the defendant was charged for ocean-freight and insurance-premium which P.W. 3 testified were paid on account of the defendant. The Bills of Lading Ext. 6 series show that the goods were consigned to the defendant-firm and contained marks B.O.M. Chittagong. The invoices also show the marks as B. O. M. Chittagong. D.W. 1's own evidence and reply to the interrogatories proves that Hridoy Ranjan Choudhury was his manager in 1958 and had authority to make the correspondences on behalf of the firm. His history that Zakir Hossain was separate from him and was doing business at Rajsbahi and Dinajpur for 20 years is ridiculous and absurd since according to his own evidence Zakir Hossain is aged 20/25 years only D.W 1 has proved himself to be a liar and no reliance can be placed on his words that Zakir Hossain had no authority in doing anything on behalf of the mill D W. 2 is a broker who does not appear to be particularly interested in the plaintiff has said that Zakir Hossain was doing the business of the mill at that time and we do not find any reason to disbelieve D W. 2. It has, therefore, been very satisfactorily proved that both Hridoy anjan Chowdhury and Zakir Hossain who are the authors of Exts. 2(d) and 2(e) had authority to look after the affairs of the defendant-firm and to make purchases and con-firm purchases through letters as done through Exts. 2(d) and 2(e) on behalf of the firm The plaintiff has proved by over-whelming evidence, oral and documentary, that there has been a contract of purchase of 1400 bags of rape-seed 700 bags @ 85/7/9 and 700 bags ®85/15/9 both F.O.B. Karachi as alleged and the defence denial of the contract is a denial for the sake of denial. The plaintiff has also proved by cogent evidence that after the shipping documents reached Chittagong, the defendant was intimated over telephone, through 'letter and also lawyer's notice but the defendant never came forward to retire the shipping documents and take delivery of the goods. It has been proved that on the failure of the defendant to retire the documents and take delivery of the goods, the plaintiff was compelled to get their names substituted in the bills of lading in place Of the, defendant, take delivery of the goods and sell the same at a controlled rate. It has also been proved by cogent evidence, oral and documentary, that the plaintiff has suffered a loss of Rs. 39,752/5/6 on account of the failure of the defendant to retire the shipping documents on payment of the in-voice dues in spite of repeated requests. Unless there was any legal impediment, the plaintiff was entitled to get the decree which the learned Subordinate Judge has passed.
